blocks.text: This video shows how to put an animation from Pixodesk 2D Animator on a web page, as a dot Lottie file. It takes one package, one canvas and a few lines of script. Let's start with the page as it is.

blocks.alt: A heading, and nothing that moves yet.

blocks.text: A heading, and nothing that moves yet. To play dot Lottie files, the page needs the dot Lottie player. Let's install it.

blocks.alt: The dot Lottie web player is in, one package.

blocks.text: The dot Lottie web player is in, one package. Now for the animation itself. Let's switch to the editor, where a football is already drawn.

blocks.alt: It's a vector drawing, standing still.

blocks.text: It's a vector drawing, standing still. To make it move, let's switch on Auto mode.

blocks.alt: With Auto mode on, every change becomes a keyframe.

blocks.text: With Auto mode on, every change becomes a keyframe. Half a second in, let's drag the ball down to the floor.

blocks.alt: A keyframe appears on the timeline, holding the new position.

blocks.text: A keyframe appears on the timeline, holding the new position. At one second, let's bring it back up.

blocks.alt: Now it falls and rises again, in one second.

blocks.text: Now it falls and rises again, in one second. A real ball speeds up as it falls, and slows down as it rises. Let's set that easing.

blocks.alt: Gravity easing, falling and rising, makes the bounce feel natural.

blocks.text: Gravity easing, falling and rising, makes the bounce feel natural. The animation is ready. Let's save it as a dot Lottie file, into the public folder.

blocks.alt: Dot Lottie is the compact, zipped form of a Lottie file.

blocks.text: Dot Lottie is the compact, zipped form of a Lottie file. Now, back to our page.

blocks.alt: The animation file is already there, in the public folder.

blocks.text: The animation file is already there, in the public folder. Let's add a canvas to the page, for the player to draw on.

blocks.alt: This player draws on a canvas, not with SVG.

blocks.text: This player draws on a canvas, not with SVG. Then, in the script, let's import the player.

blocks.alt: It comes from the dot Lottie web package.

blocks.text: It comes from the dot Lottie web package. And start it on the canvas, with the animation file.

blocks.alt: It takes the canvas, the file's address, and loop and autoplay.

blocks.text: It takes the canvas, the file's address, and loop and autoplay. Let's reload the page, and watch.

blocks.alt: There it is. The ball bounces, drawn on the canvas.

blocks.text: There it is. The ball bounces, drawn on the canvas. So, one package, one dot Lottie file saved from the editor, a canvas, and a few lines of script. That's all it takes to bring an animation onto a web page.
